item.title: CRISPR-based Cellgorithm technology ushers in a new era of cell programming
item.description: Syntax Bio, a synthetic biology company programming the next generation of cell therapies, today announced the publication of new research in Science Advances detailing the company's CRISPR-based Cellgorithm technology, which lays the groundwork for programmable control of gene activity in human stem cells and offers an alternative to the slow, variable manual processes researchers use today.

item.title: Study finds mixed reviews of virtual nursing programs among bedside nurses
item.description: Hospitals struggling to attract and retain enough registered nurses at the bedside are implementing alternative strategies to ensure patients get needed nursing care.

item.title: Phonological processing skills continue to influence text reading fluency in adolescents
item.description: Psycholinguists from the Center for Language and Brain found that phonological processing skills continue to influence text reading fluency in 15-to-18-year-old adolescents.

item.title: New Lancet series blends social science with medicine to tackle global health inequities
item.description: Can doctors in California learn from a patient who was bounced from one specialist to another in Japan? Can clinicians in London take lessons from a patient seeking asylum while suffering a medical emergency at the U.S.-Mexico border? Can doctors treating refugees in Africa inform health policy around the world?

item.title: Protein network locks ABCC4 transporters in place to maintain cyclic AMP signaling levels
item.description: When a cell receives a message from outside, it generates a molecule called cyclic AMP (cAMP) to relay this message. To ensure the signal reaches the correct effector without triggering pathways accidentally, cAMP levels must be maintained around their point of origin and at the right level.

item.title: In RFK Jr.’s upside-down world of vaccines, panel votes to end hepatitis B shot at birth
item.description: Recent weeks have brought good news about vaccines, with studies indicating that flu vaccination reduces heart disease, shingles vaccines can prevent or slow dementia, and a single human papilloma virus shot protects a girl from cervical cancer for the rest of her life.

item.title: Brainwide circuitry mapping reveals how psilocybin drives therapeutic neural rewiring
item.description: An international collaboration led by Cornell University researchers used a combination of psilocybin and the rabies virus to map how – and where – the psychedelic compound rewires the connections in the brain.

item.title: WHO Member States push forward toward a unified Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing system
item.description: WHO Member States today ended their latest round of intensive negotiations on the world's first Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing (PABS) system.

item.title: Billions still lack essential health services despite worldwide gains in coverage
item.description: Since 2000, most countries – across all income levels and regions – have made concurrent progress in expanding health service coverage and reducing the financial hardship associated with health costs, according to a new joint report from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the World Bank Group.

item.title: Exa-cel shows complete success in early pediatric trials for sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia
item.description: Preliminary results from two trials of the gene therapy exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel) suggest the therapy offers an effective cure for beta-thalassemia and sickle cell disease in children younger than 12.
